newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Annan says he humbled by choice as U.N. leader.
newsitem.headline: Annan says he humbled by choice as U.N. leader.

text.p: Kofi Annan, the low-key chief of United Nations peacekeeping forces, maintained his legendary poise on Friday as he was picked as the U.N.'s seventh general secretary, a move that ended a bruising diplomatic war.

While staff in his 37th floor U.N. office broke out champagne and literally jumped for joy, Annan was an oasis of calm. He smiled, accepted handshakes, posed for pictures and appeared so blase about his triumph that one long-time aides said, "He looked like that happened every day of his life."

The only sign of excitement the aide could discern was that the 58-year-old diplomat from Ghana shifted his weight slightly from foot to foot -- "That's what he does when he shows emotion," one staff member said.

Security guards, dressed in light U.N. blue uniforms, immediately raced to Annan's office to protect him but the man who headed peacekeeping operations from Bosnia to Rwanda to Cambodia hardly seemed to notice.
"It is very humbling and a great honour," Annan said in an interview with Reuters shortly afterwards, speaking in almost hushed tones.
He noted proudly that he was the first man from sub-Sahara Africa to be named secretary general and pledged,
"Even though my base is Africa, I will be a secretary general for the whole world. The secretary general ... does have a moral voice that has to be heard," he said.
"The continent will see this (his selection) as an honour. I have had phone calls from Ghana over the last few days saying that the whole country was rooting for me," he added.
Although he won his new post with strong U.S. and British backing, overcoming days of French objections, Annan promised to be independent.

"The secretary general must have an independent judgment. There will be times when the secretary general and the security council will not agree and I hope that the disagreements will not be acrimonious."

Annan's selection elated the much-criticised U.N. bureaucracy, ending a battle that pitted France against the United States and Britain and giving outgoing U.S. Ambassador Madeleine Albright a triumph before she takes over as U.S. Secretary of State.

Washington had undiplomatically blocked a second term for Egypt's Boutros Boutros-Ghali, whose leadership became a campaign issue in the U.S. presidential election amid harsh Republican criticism of the United Nations.

Many in the world organisation bristled that the Clinton administration had decioded to get rid of a good diplomat for no good reason -- Bob Dole's making fun of the name "Boutros Boutros-Ghali." But Annan's choice helps mute that criticism.
As the first professional U.N. bureaucrat to win the world organisation's top job, his choice was popular with both those who work with him and those he works for.

France, which has been picking fights with the United States recently, was not willing to let Boutros-Ghali go quietly and it boldly confronted the United States by holding out against Annan for days.
French diplomats and sources close to Annan both noted the criticism was not personnel and said he had worked well with France in the past and expected to do so in the future.

The United States was unable to campaign openly for Annan because of widespread anger at its veto of Boutros-Ghali so the task was left to British envoys who were in the forefront of lobbying the 15-member Security Council, diplomats said..
British U.N. ambassador Sir John Weston was the first to announce the news that the council had reached agreement on Annan's candidacy.

Annan pledged to continue reforms of the world body, saying that an organisation that is 50 years old could benefit from changes. He added that he hoped to convince the United States to pay its $1.4 billion debt to the U.N. and said it was hurting the small countries who have not been paid for sending peacekeeping troops around the world.

He said he would have a brief holiday once the General Assembly affirmed the Security Council's decision -- but he quietly refused to say where that would be. Instead, he joked, "Let's talk about English football. I like Manchester United."
